extracted_facts: Project management SaaS targeting small teams
~5,000 users expected in the first year, EU-based
Real-time notifications and live collaboration now required in v1
ambiguities: Assumed WebSocket-based live updates rather than polling
Assumed collaboration means presence + task updates, not full document co-editing

options.name: Serverless + WebSocket
options.summary: Lambda + API Gateway WebSocket APIs with DynamoDB. Fully managed real-time at pay-per-use pricing.
options.rationale: API Gateway WebSocket APIs remove the hardest part of real-time (connection management) and keep the pay-per-use economics.

pros: Managed WebSocket connections — no server state to track
tradeoffs.best_when: Real-time is a feature, not the product, and you want zero ops.

assumptions: 5,000 users, ~30% concurrently connected during work hours

options.name: Fargate + Redis Pub/Sub
options.summary: The recommended container stack extended with WebSocket support on the ALB and Redis Pub/Sub for fan-out.
options.rationale: ALBs natively support WebSocket, so real-time rides on the same containers you already run. Redis Pub/Sub fans messages across tasks without adding a new managed service.

pros: One stack for HTTP and WebSocket
PostgreSQL still fits the data model
Redis Pub/Sub is battle-tested for this exact use case
Incremental: ship CRUD first, add sockets later
cons: WebSocket connections pin tasks — autoscaling must account for connection draining
~$30-50/month more than v1 for the Redis upgrade
tradeoffs.best_when: You want real-time inside a familiar relational stack without new service categories.

options.scalability_ceiling: ~30,000 concurrent connections before needing a dedicated broker (e.g., managed MQTT or ElastiCache cluster mode)
options.security_posture: Strong; private subnets, WAF, KMS encryption, TLS on sockets

options.name: Managed Real-Time (AppSync)
options.summary: Fargate core for CRUD plus AWS AppSync subscriptions for real-time — real-time as a managed service.
options.rationale: AppSync subscriptions handle connection management, fan-out, and auth integration with Cognito out of the box — you write GraphQL resolvers, not socket code.

pros: GraphQL schema gives clients a typed contract
cons: GraphQL learning curve if the team is REST-native
AppSync pricing grows with subscription minutes
Adds a second API surface to maintain
tradeoffs.best_when: You want managed real-time and are open to GraphQL.

options.scalability_ceiling: Very high; AppSync subscriptions scale to millions of connections
options.security_posture: Strong; Cognito-authorized subscriptions, private VPC resources

recommendation.rationale: With real-time now in v1, the container option extends most naturally: the ALB already terminates WebSockets, and Redis Pub/Sub is the simplest correct way to fan out messages across Fargate tasks. You keep PostgreSQL for the relational core, add no new service categories, and can ship CRUD first and sockets second. AppSync is excellent but forces a GraphQL migration your team didn't ask for; serverless WebSocket remains cheapest but inherits the DynamoDB modeling risk flagged in v1.

why_not_others.reason: Still the cheapest, but the DynamoDB modeling risk for relational project/task data remains, and WebSocket-on-Lambda debugging is materially harder for a small team.
AppSync subscriptions are the most scalable path, but introducing GraphQL now adds a learning curve and a second API surface before product-market fit is proven.
